topicName: Redis Cluster Hash Slots (16384) and Sharding
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Redis Cluster Hash Slots (16384) and Sharding"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis Cluster provides a way to run a Redis installation where data is automatically sharded across multiple Redis nodes. Understanding how Redis handles data distribution via hash slots is crucial for scaling your database architecture efficiently."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is a Hash Slot?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike traditional consistent hashing implementations, Redis Cluster uses the concept of hash slots. The entire database space is divided into a fixed total of 16384 hash slots. Every key in a Redis Cluster belongs to one of these hash slots."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Total number of hash slots: 16384."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Each master node in a Redis Cluster is assigned a subset of these hash slots."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The formula used to calculate the hash slot for a given key is HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"Why Exactly 16384 Hash Slots?"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The choice of 16384 (which is 2^14) slots is a deliberate design decision balancing cluster state communication efficiency and memory overhead. Redis nodes communicate frequently to share cluster state, known as cluster bus packets. These packets contain the bitmap of which slots are owned by which node."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"With 16384 slots, the bitmap takes 2KB of memory (16384 / 8 bits = 2048 bytes)."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"If it were 65536 slots (2^16), the bitmap would require 8KB, consuming significantly more network bandwidth for heartbeat packets."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Redis Clusters typically do not scale efficiently beyond 1000 master nodes, making 16384 slots more than adequate for granular distribution."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Hash Tags for Multi-Key Operations"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"By default, every key is hashed independently. This means multi-key operations (like MGET or transactions) will fail if the keys hash to different slots managed by different nodes. To force specific keys to reside in the same hash slot, Redis provides Hash Tags."},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"If there is a substring inside braces '{}' in a key, only what is inside the braces is hashed. For example, 'user:{1000}:profile' and 'user:{1000}:settings' will both be hashed based strictly on '1000', guaranteeing they fall into the exact same hash slot."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"SET user:{1000}:profile \"John Doe\"\nSET user:{1000}:settings \"dark_mode\"\nMGET user:{1000}:profile user:{1000}:settings"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Resharding and Slot Migration"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"When scaling out a Redis Cluster by adding new nodes, you must move hash slots from existing nodes to the new node. This process is called resharding and is managed using the 'redis-cli --cluster reshard' utility."},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"redis-cli --cluster reshard 127.0.0.1:7000"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"During migration, slots transition through states such as MIGRATING on the source node and IMPORTING on the destination node, ensuring zero downtime for read and write operations during normal cluster rebalancing."}]
